summary: Sets out terminology and operational requirements for interoperability among multiple Public Key Infrastructure domains, each with its own policy. It describes relationships between certification authorities, defines PKI domains, and discusses typical multi-domain models. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Different groups issue ID cards under different rules. This paper gives shared words and rules so the groups can trust each other's cards.

questions: how do different cas establish trust
subtitle: Making different digital ID systems trust each other across organizations.

tldr.problem: When different organizations each run their own Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to issue digital certificates, they need clear terminology and rules to establish trust across PKI boundaries so that a certificate from one PKI can be accepted by another.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines PKI domain concepts, describes how Certification Authorities establish trust via cross-certificates, and outlines multi-domain PKI architectures (hierarchical, mesh, hybrid) and trust models.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now set up inter-domain trust relationships systematically, avoiding inadvertent trust chains and supporting secure interoperability.

today: RFC 5217 is informational and provides foundational guidance on PKI domain concepts. It remains relevant for organizations designing multi-domain PKI systems, although modern use cases often rely on centralized Certificate Authorities and web-based trust models. The RFC has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Multiple PKIs and Multi-Domain Trust
sections.content:
A Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is a system where a trusted authority (a Certification Authority or CA) issues digital certificates binding a person's or entity's identity to a public key. Most organizations run their own PKI under their own policy.

When two organizations want to work together, they need to establish trust so that a certificate from one PKI can be validated by the other. This is done using cross-certificates—a certificate issued by one CA to another CA, signaling trust. A PKI domain is a collection of multiple PKIs that have entered into such trust relationships. This RFC provides terminology and operational requirements for building and maintaining multi-domain PKIs.
sections.plainLanguage: One company issues ID cards (a PKI). Another company does the same. Now they want to say 'I trust the other company's ID cards'. That agreement is a multi-domain PKI.

sections.title: How CAs Trust Each Other
sections.content:
Certification Authorities build trust relationships in two ways. Hierarchical relationships have a parent CA and child CAs in a tree. A root CA sits at the top with a self-signed certificate and issues certificates to subordinate CAs, which in turn issue to end entities. A Unifying CA is similar but uses one-way cross-certificates instead of subordinate certificates, allowing child CAs to keep self-signed roots.

Peer-to-peer relationships have no parent-child hierarchy. Cross-certificates are mutual (bilateral) or one-way (unilateral). In a mesh, all CAs may cross-certify each other (full mesh) or only some (partial mesh). A Bridge CA is a neutral intermediary that only manages cross-certificates, not end-entity certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Hierarchical: one CA at the top signs for everyone below it. Mesh: all CAs sign for each other. Bridge: a referee who mediates between others.

sections.title: Organizing Multi-Domain PKI
sections.content:
A PKI domain is formally defined by governance documents (memoranda, charters, policy statements) that establish the domain's purpose, members, authority, and rules. Each member PKI retains its own Certificate Policy OID (a unique identifier for its rules) but also asserts a domain Policy OID shared across the domain.

Trust anchors (the root certificates trusted by relying parties) vary by architecture. In a single-CA PKI, the one CA is the trust anchor. In a hierarchical domain, the root CA is the trust anchor. In a mesh, each member can be a trust anchor. A Principal CA (designated by each PKI) manages trust relationships with other domains.

A critical requirement: when a PKI joins multiple domains, it must inform all domains of its memberships to prevent inadvertent trust chains. For example, if PKI-A trusts PKI-B and PKI-B trusts PKI-C, but A and C should not trust each other, cross-certificates must include constraints (policy mappings or name constraints) to block the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Each group writes down its rules. When groups team up, they say 'I trust groups A, B, C but NOT their friends'. That way you don't accidentally trust someone you didn't mean to.

sections.title: Multi-Domain Models
sections.content:
Hierarchical architecture: A root CA at the top issues certificates to subordinate CAs below. Simple to understand, but the root CA is a single point of failure. Easy to manage constraints.

Mesh architecture: CAs are peers, issuing cross-certificates to each other. A full mesh connects every CA to every other (scalable but complex). A partial mesh has fewer connections (simpler, but trust paths may not exist between all CAs).

Hybrid architecture: Combines hierarchy and mesh. Some CAs are subordinate; others are peers cross-certifying. Useful for organizations merging over time. Can become very complex.

Unifying domain model: Establishes a joint superior CA that cross-certifies each member domain's Principal CA, creating a unified point of trust without restructuring member domains. Relying parties that want cross-domain trust switch to the Unifying CA; others use their original trust anchor.
sections.plainLanguage: Hierarchy: one boss at top. Mesh: all equal, all sign for each other. Hybrid: some hierarchy, some equality. Unifying: a new super-boss coordinates everyone.

sections.title: Trust Lists and Relying Parties
sections.content:
A relying party (an entity that validates a certificate) must decide which CAs to trust. A Trust List is a set of trust anchors. Two models manage them. In a Local Trust List Model, each relying party maintains its own list (decentralized). In a Trust Authority Model, a central trusted entity publishes the list (centralized).

The Local Trust List model is flexible but requires each relying party to manage updates. The Trust Authority model is simpler for users but introduces a central point of control. In a multi-domain PKI, relying parties may use different models; the PKI domain documentation should clarify expectations.
sections.plainLanguage: Local: everyone has their own list of who to trust. Authority: one person publishes the list and everyone uses it.
